query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount (~0.1 at.%) of boron to the equal‐atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW alloy will promote the formation of nanoscale boride precipitates at grain boundaries that enhance cohesion. This intervention is expected to improve the alloy’s room‐temperature ductility and mitigate irradiation-induced damage (such as helium blistering and amorphization) while preserving its high-temperature BCC stability and exceptional strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal‐atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW alloy that exhibits excellent high-temperature strength (up to 1600 °C) but poor room-temperature ductility and uncertain irradiation tolerance.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor doping (~0.1 at.%) of boron during alloy synthesis with controlled thermal processing to encourage intergranular boride precipitation.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing at room temperature and high temperatures (up to ~1600 °C) along with irradiation experiments (e.g., helium ion implantation or dual-beam irradiation at reactor-relevant temperatures around 900–1073 K and damage levels up to ~8 dpa or ~9% He implantation).
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale boride precipitates that form preferentially at grain boundaries, thereby improving local cohesion and acting as defect sinks during irradiation.
generation.mechanism: The added boron reacts during processing to form coherent or semi-coherent boride phases at the grain boundaries. This improves grain-boundary cohesion and alters the local stress fields, promoting more uniform plastic deformation at room temperature (increasing ductility) and providing sites for helium or irradiation-induced defects to be trapped, thus reducing blistering, amorphization, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation. The BCC matrix remains largely intact to maintain high-temperature strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the boron-doped variant should exhibit a significant improvement in room-temperature ductility (e.g., higher elongation and altered fracture mode from intergranular to more transgranular failure), while retaining its high-temperature mechanical performance. In irradiation tests, reduced helium bubble coalescence, lower hardening fractions, and fewer surface instabilities (blistering or amorphization) are expected.
generation.baseline: Untreated equal-atomic NbMoTaW, which offers excellent high-temperature performance but suffers from poor ductility at room temperature and potential phase- or surface-instability under irradiation conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are anticipated to hold under service temperatures from room temperature up to ~1600 °C and under irradiation conditions typical for reactor environments (up to ~8 dpa and ~9% helium implantation).
generation.uncertainty: The hypothesis extrapolates from studies that demonstrated boron-induced intergranular boride precipitation improving ductility in other refractory high-entropy alloys (e.g., HfMoNbTaTiZr) and from irradiation studies showing defect trapping by second-phase particles in similar BCC alloys. It is uncertain how the exact boride morphology, precipitate distribution, and potential interactions with high-temperature creep behavior will manifest in NbMoTaW; these factors require experimental optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of NbMoTaW alloy – one processed with ~0.1 at.% boron addition and a control without boron – using identical synthesis and controlled cooling protocols. Characterize the microstructure (using TEM and atom probe tomography) to verify the formation of nanoscale boride precipitates at grain boundaries. Perform room-temperature tensile and compressive tests, high-temperature mechanical tests (up to 1600 °C), and irradiation experiments (e.g., helium ion implantation or dual-beam irradiation at 900–1073 K to doses comparable to ~8 dpa or ~9% He content). Compare ductility, hardness, and irradiation-induced microstructural evolution between the doped and undoped samples.
measurements: High-temperature strength retention and phase stability
Grain-boundary chemistry and precipitate distribution (via TEM/APT)
Irradiation hardening, helium bubble density/size, and surface blistering metrics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped NbMoTaW alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in ductility at room temperature and reduced irradiation damage (as evidenced by similar or worse helium bubble formation, hardening, or surface instabilities) without compromising its high-temperature strength compared to the undoped control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In summary, careful microstructural examination of Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr was carried out in the present study using advanced TEM and APT techniques. The results reveal that the homogenized and slow cooled (~10 °C/min) microstructure (Condition (1)) has an ordered B2 phase as the continuous matrix, interspersed with discrete cuboidal-like pockets of a disordered BCC phase. While this microstructure morphologically resembles the γ (fcc) + γ’ (ordered L12) type microstructure observed in many Ni-base superalloys, it is “inverted” in the sense that the continuous matrix phase is the ordered B2 phase, resulting in limited compressive ductility. The ductility of this alloy was substantially increased via microstructural engineering involving controlled annealing treatments, resulting in a phase inversion. Consequently, the hard, ordered B2 compound that forms the continuous phase in Condition (1) is replaced by the more ductile, disordered, BCC phase in Condition (3). The resultant microstructurally-engineered RHEA not only exhibits high yield strength at room temperature (~1345 MPa) and 600 °C (~1423 MPa), but also substantial compressive ductility at room temperature (>20%). However, material microstructures can be engineered to tolerate the helium irradiation environment to mitigate the effects of He bubble accumulation. Strategies for limiting helium bubble effects in metals include decreasing the grain size [,], intentionally controlling the columnar microstructure [,], alloying [,], and introducing second phase interfaces/interphases [,,]. Trapping He bubbles at the second phase precipitates or at interfaces in layered composites can mitigate the He effects in the matrix and may be more stable at high temperatures. Grain boundaries are strong traps for He bubbles and increasing the grain boundary density has been shown to reduce the number of intergranular He bubbles, thus reducing the swelling risk [,]. However, He accumulation will change the mechanical properties; additionally, nanocrystalline metals with a high grain boundary (GB) density are unstable at high temperatures and prone to grain growth [,].

Boron has also been widely added in alloys to improve the cohesive strength of grain boundaries [], e.g., to change the fracture mode of Ni3Al from intergranular to transgranular and thus prevent early failure [], or to lower the migration rate of grain boundaries and inhibit grain growth at high temperatures []. Additionally, the short-range order in an Fe40Mn40Co10Cr10 alloy caused by the addition of boron atoms or the precipitation of borides was reported to retard the motion and increase the density of dislocations [], and the discontinuous intergranular precipitation of borides in high-strength steels avoided the intergranular fracture [], both improving the mechanical properties of the alloys [,]. As the grain-boundary brittleness is a major issue for BCC RHEAs, a minor amount of boron element (0.1 at.%) was hence added into an HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA in the present study for potential precipitation of borides at the grain boundaries and improvement of grain boundary cohesion, then to yield a larger work hardenability and better ductility.
